source.filename: 2019-Superelastic NiTi SMA cables Thermal-mechanical behavior, hysteretic modelling and seismic application.pdf

constitutive_assumptions: Austenite-to-martensite solid-to-solid phase transformation behavior modeled using one-dimensional flag-shaped hysteretic formulation.
Cable cross-section equivalent to an idealized circular section partitioned into multiple concentric fiber layers under uniaxial stress.
Central core layer modeled with isotropic hardening steel (Steel02) with identical yield strength to SMA to capture residual strain and cyclic degradation.
Outer three layers modeled with Self-centering material behavior possessing graded Young's modulus reduction factors (k0) to represent non-synchronized wire tension.
Displacement-based fiber beam-column elements assume plane sections remain plane for the bridge pier.
Reinforcing steel follows the Menegotto-Pinto constitutive law with linear kinematic and zero isotropic hardening; concrete follows the Kent-Scott-Park model for confined and unconfined sections.
Frictional sliding bearings modeled as ideal elastic-plastic behavior in zero-length spring elements.
Cables resist tension only; compressive buckling is neglected and slack displacement is accounted for using zero-length gap elements in series.
control_variables: Cable construction: 7 x 7 configuration (7 strands consisting of 7 wires each; total 49 monofilament wires)
Wire diameter: 0.8 mm (measured outer cable diameter approx. 7 mm; specimen total length approx. 350 mm)
Material composition: commercial Ti-50.8at.%Ni ingot processed by hot-working, cold-working (30-40% area reduction), and straightening (450 °C for 30 s)
Furnace heat treatment followed immediately by water quenching
Quasi-static tensile loading rate: displacement control at 5 mm/min on Universal Test Machine (UTM)
Testing ambient temperature: room temperature of approximately 28 °C
End constraint: thin epoxy coating on cable ends clamped in matching hydraulic wedge grips
Digital Image Correlation (DIC) camera sampling rate at 0.5 Hz with speckled surface paint treatment
dependent_variables: Phase transformation temperatures (martensitic start/finish Ms, Mf, and austenitic start/finish As, Af, and intermediate R-phase temperatures)
Forward transformation start stress (yield strength) and forward transformation finish stress
Peak stress at maximum global strain
Accumulated residual strain and recovery rate (self-centering capability)
Equivalent viscous damping ratio (EVD) (energy dissipation capability)
Form setting ability (resistance to unravelling after mid-span cutting)
Peak and residual girder displacements in seismic time-history bridge analysis

evidence_relevant_to_topic.claim: Monofilament NiTi wires annealed at moderate temperatures (400-450 °C for 15 min) exhibit flag-shaped superelastic responses recovering over 90% of strain after undergoing 8% maximum strain, but suffer transformation-induced fatigue (TIF) and residual strain accumulation under cyclic loading.

7 x 7 superelastic SMA cables scale up wire properties but demonstrate smoother, more gradual phase transformation transitions due to non-uniform stress states (combining tension, torsion, and bending) and out-of-sync wire engagement across the bundled cross-section.

Annealing schemes significantly modify phase transformation temperatures: moderate annealing (350-450 °C) maintains Af close to or below room temperature, whereas high annealing (500-550 °C) lowers Af down to -20 °C, inducing over-aging and degrading superelastic recovery.
Annealing at 400 °C or higher for 15 minutes followed by water quenching provides full form setting (shape setting), preventing stranded 7 x 7 SMA cables from unravelling when cut.
Pre-training SMA cables for approximately five constant-strain cycles stabilizes hysteretic response and limits further residual strain accumulation, capturing over 80% of final residual deformation.

An empirical multi-layer modeling approach combining concentric self-centering SMA fiber layers with stiffness reduction factors and an inner isotropic hardening steel core accurately simulates the out-of-sync wire tension, loop shape, and cyclic degradation of SMA cables.
Digital Image Correlation (DIC) enables reliable non-contact full-field strain measurement on stranded SMA cables where physical extensometers slip due to cable bending and slack during unloading.

experimental_setup: Differential Scanning Calorimetry (DSC) with cooling-heating cycles at 10 °C/min to measure transformation temperatures.
Electrical furnace used for annealing wires and cables at 350 °C to 550 °C followed by water quenching.
Universal Test Machine (UTM) equipped with hydraulic wedge grips and built-in load cell for uniaxial tensile cyclic testing under displacement control (5 mm/min).
Epoxy end coating on cable specimens to prevent clamping-induced stress concentrations and end failures.
Non-contact GOM Digital Image Correlation (DIC) double-camera system tracking surface speckle pattern at 0.5 Hz to measure local strain fields.
Mid-span cutting evaluation of post-cyclic cable specimens to assess form setting and unravelling resistance.
future_work: Testing larger-diameter SMA cables and calibrating numerical models to reduce the required number of physical restrainers.
Evaluating seismic response under a wider and more diverse suite of earthquake ground motions.
Developing a comprehensive performance-based design framework for structures incorporating SMA-cable restrainers.
independent_variables: Cyclic loading protocol (incremental strain loading from 1% to 10% strain; constant strain cyclic loading at 6% or 10% strain for 20 cycles)
Specimen morphology (monofilament wire vs. 7 x 7 multi-strand cable)
limitations_inferred: The proposed multi-layer fiber section modeling approach relies on empirical trial-and-error fitting of area fractions and stiffness reduction factors rather than an analytical mechanics-based formulation derived from cable geometry.
Experimental testing was restricted to quasi-static loading (5 mm/min) at room temperature (28 °C), omitting dynamic strain-rate effects and thermal self-heating during rapid cycling.
High-cycle structural fatigue leading to mechanical fracture was not evaluated.
The study targets civil engineering bridge restrainers and does not examine robotic implementations, multi-axis bending, sheath friction, or miniaturized robotic actuators.
limitations_stated_by_authors: The numerical simulation model for single SMA wires does not account for cyclic degradation effects.
Minor discrepancies remain between numerical simulations and experimental results along the cable unloading paths.
Physical contact extensometers are unsuitable for SMA cable testing because bending deformation during unloading causes leg slippage.
Minor slippage at clamped ends is inevitable in cable tension testing at large strain levels.
SMA cables exhibit lower equivalent viscous damping ratios (2-6%) than monofilament wires (7%+) due to non-synchronized wire deformation.
The numerical case study is limited to an illustrative analysis using a single unscaled ground motion record (El Centro EW) without a comprehensive performance-based design framework.
Larger diameter cables require future experimental verification and model calibration before practical adoption.
main_results: 7 x 7 superelastic NiTi SMA cables successfully scale up the load-carrying capacity of SMA wires while producing smoother stress-strain curves due to multi-axial stress states and non-synchronized wire engagement.
Moderate annealing (350-400 °C for 15 min) enhances cable stiffness, energy dissipation, and form setting, whereas overly high annealing (>= 500 °C) causes over-aging and degrades superelasticity.
Annealing at 400 °C or above for 15 min imparts complete form setting, preventing 7 x 7 cables from unravelling after cutting.
Initial cable elastic modulus ranges from 30 to 45 GPa, increasing with annealing temperature and decreasing with cycle number.
Yield strength of cables degrades by over 20% across 20 cycles (dropping below 400 MPa), while peak stress remains stable and immune to cyclic degradation.
Recovery rates exceed 80-85% (residual strains < 1.5% after 10% strain) for properly annealed cables, but drop to 67% for cables annealed at 500 °C.
Over 80% of cumulative residual strain occurs within the first 5 cycles, indicating that mechanical pre-training effectively stabilizes cable hysteretic behavior.
Equivalent viscous damping ratio (EVD) of the cables ranges between 2% and 6%.
The proposed multi-layer SMA and steel fiber OpenSees model reliably captures the flag-shaped hysteresis, non-synchronous wire engagement, and yield degradation of SMA cables.

In a two-span RC bridge case study, SMA-cable restrainers reduced peak girder displacement from 185 mm to 85 mm and residual girder displacement from 142 mm to 34 mm under the El Centro ground motion.
modeling_methods: Displacement-based nonlinear fiber beam-column elements in OpenSees.
Multi-layer concentric fiber approach combining Self-centering SMA material and Steel02 isotropic hardening steel material.
Zero-length gap elements placed in series to capture cable slack displacement.
Uniaxial Menegotto-Pinto constitutive modeling for reinforcing steel bars.
Kent-Scott-Park uniaxial constitutive modeling for confined and unconfined concrete.
Zero-length spring elements with ideal elastic-plastic behavior for sliding bearings and soil-structure interaction (SSI).
Nonlinear dynamic time-history analysis under unscaled earthquake ground motion (El Centro EW).
performance_metrics: Transformation temperatures: Ms, Mf, As, Af, and R-phase peak temperatures (°C)
Forward transformation start stress / yield strength (MPa) and finish stress (MPa)
Reverse transformation start and finish stresses (MPa)
Accumulated residual strain (%) and recovery rate (%)
Peak girder displacement (mm) and residual girder displacement (mm)
possible_gap_implications: The demonstrated form setting and pre-training stabilization of 7 x 7 NiTi cables provides practical guidance for designing flexible, kink-resistant, self-centering tendons in tendon-driven continuum robots and variable-stiffness compliant joints.

The multi-layer concentric fiber formulation offers a computationally efficient 1D hysteretic framework that could be adapted to simulate non-synchronous wire engagement and cyclic degradation in robotic cable transmissions without requiring 3D solid FE contact models.

Because the paper evaluates only quasi-static tension in large civil restrainers, research gaps remain regarding the high-speed cyclic fatigue, localized bending/friction against guide conduits, and dynamic actuation control of SMA cables in robotic mechanisms.
paper.research_objective: To comprehensively investigate the thermal-mechanical behavior, annealing scheme influences, form setting characteristics, and hysteretic properties of 7 x 7 superelastic NiTi SMA cables; to propose an effective numerical hysteretic modeling approach; and to evaluate the seismic damage mitigation performance of SMA-cable restrainers in a model bridge structure.
paper.research_problem: Monofilament SMA wires possess insufficient load resistance and difficult end-gripping for large-scale structural applications, while SMA bars suffer from inferior mechanical properties, machining notch sensitivity, and brittle failure modes; furthermore, the effects of heat treatment (annealing) on the phase transformation, hysteretic behavior, form setting, and numerical simulation of multi-strand superelastic SMA cables remain insufficiently explored.
stiffness_mechanism: solid-to-solid phase transformation between austenite and martensite phases (superelasticity)
heat treatment (annealing) induced microstructure and elastic modulus modification
paper.title: Superelastic NiTi SMA cables: Thermal-mechanical behavior, hysteretic modelling and seismic application
